 KRA’s April tax deadline: Why Kenyans must stop waiting until the last minute
 Saturday 14th November, 2026 06:23 PM | 
 By Sharon Atieno 
 KRA office building. PHOTO/@KRACorporate/X 
 The Kenya Revenue Authority’s decision to move the deadline for filing individual income tax returns from June 30 to April 30 is more than a change to the tax calendar. It is a reminder that taxpayers must rethink how they manage their financial records throughout the year.
 From January 1, 2027, individuals filing their 2026 income tax returns will have to submit them by April 30, 2027 two months earlier than under the previous arrangement.
 For many Kenyans, filing returns has become an annual rush, with taxpayers scrambling to retrieve employment records, confirm tax deductions and resolve discrepancies as the June deadline approaches. The new date leaves less room for procrastination and makes early preparation increasingly important.
 Tax compliance should not be a last-minute exercise
 One of the biggest mistakes taxpayers make is treating annual returns as a task to be handled only when the deadline approaches.
 Employees may assume that their employer has already handled everything because Pay As You Earn (PAYE) tax is deducted from their salaries every month. However, taxpayers still need to understand their individual filing obligations and ensure the information submitted to KRA is accurate.
 Kenya Revenue Authority officials review digital property records during a rental-income compliance check 
 Employment income records, tax deduction certificates and other relevant documents should be kept throughout the year rather than collected in a panic weeks before the deadline.
 For self-employed Kenyans and people with additional sources of income, proper record-keeping is even more important. Waiting until April to reconstruct an entire year’s financial activity can lead to mistakes, omissions and unnecessary anxiety.
 An earlier deadline demands better taxpayer awareness
 The revised deadline also raises questions about how effectively taxpayers will be informed and supported during the transition.
 KRA should ensure that clear, accessible guidance reaches employees, small business owners, freelancers and other individual taxpayers well before the new deadline takes effect. Public education should explain who is required to file, which documents are needed and how taxpayers can correct errors before submission.
 An earlier deadline should not become a trap for people who are unaware of the change or struggle to access the relevant information.
 Tax compliance works best when obligations are clearly communicated and taxpayers have the practical means to meet them.
 Make April 30 a deadline, not a deadline-day emergency
 Kenyans should begin organising their 2026 income records early, confirm their filing requirements and seek clarification from KRA whenever they are unsure.
 Employers can also help by making relevant tax documents available promptly, while taxpayers should avoid relying on assumptions that deductions from their salaries automatically settle every filing obligation.
 A woman files her tax returns on the KRA website. Image used for illustration 
 Ultimately, the change should encourage a more responsible approach to personal finances. Filing returns is not simply about meeting a statutory deadline; it is also about maintaining accurate records and understanding one’s tax obligations.
 With April 30, 2027, now the key date for filing 2026 individual income tax returns, the best strategy is straightforward: prepare early, verify the figures and file on time.
 The real test will be whether taxpayers and the authority use the change to build a simpler, better-understood culture of tax compliance rather than another annual scramble.
